title: The Matrix Revolutions
full_review:
At one point during the grandiose climax of "The Matrix Revolutions" (Warner Bros.), Smith, the film's virtual villain, experiences a sense of digital deja vu and snarls, "I've seen this before." That sentiment may be shared by the audience throughout this final installment of Larry and Andy Wachowski's bloated cyber-noir "Matrix" trilogy.

All three movies consist of protracted, ultraviolent action sequences stitched together by dollops of pretentious, pseudo-philosophical dialogue and allegorical symbolism, with over-the-top, gravity-defying brawls serving as the visual centerpiece of each movie. Though the Wachowskis rein in the existential banter in this third go-round, the stylized carnage remains at full throttle. And while the franchise continues to push the envelope of technical wizardry, it's in inverse proportion to narrative and character development.

The result is an overstuffed maelstrom of noise and violence, a sound and fury signifying nothing. Like the Matrix itself, the film looks substantial, but is ultimately empty of any real content.

For those who missed the first two films, there is a lot of plot to download, so here goes. Keanu Reeves plays Neo, a computer hacker turned reluctant messiah who discovers that what he thought was the real world was just a computer simulation piped into his brain by sentient machines which, in some distant dystopian future, have taken over the world and which keep him -- along with most of Earth's population -- imprisoned in this illusory reality known as "the Matrix" in order to harvest their neural electricity as a fuel source.

A few hundred stalwart humans have escaped to the subterranean stronghold of Zion -- the last outpost of humanity -- in the hope of overthrowing the machines. The first film, "The Matrix" (1999), chronicled how Neo was liberated by the enigmatic Morpheus (Laurence Fishburne), a brooding freedom fighter who believes Neo is "the One," the prophesized savior of humanity, and Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss), the latex-coutured hellcat who becomes Neo's lover.

The sequel, "The Matrix Reloaded" (2003), continued Neo's quest to fulfill his messianic destiny. Guided by the sage-like program The Oracle, who takes on the human form of an old woman (Mary Alice), Neo learns to channel his incredible powers to manipulate the Matrix. Neo's nemesis, the rapacious rogue program Smith (played with wicked glee by Hugo Weaving), also grows in strength, posing a threat not only to mankind, but also to the machine empire. The second film ends on a cliffhanger, with Neo comatose after saving a rebel hovercraft from an attack by Sentinels -- calamari-looking killer droids boring through the earth to lay siege to Zion, bent on the extinction of mankind.
The curtain rises on "The Matrix Revolutions" with Neo still unconscious, his mind trapped in a state of limbo between the Matrix and the real world -- cleverly depicted as an immaculately sterile subway station. Trinity, Morpheus and a kung-fu program named Seraph (Collin Chou) track down the elusive Trainman (Bruce Spence) -- the only program who can release Neo from his psychic waylay. Meanwhile, Zion prepares for an Armageddon-like last stand against an invading machine army.

Once reawakened -- at least we think he's conscious, though with Reeves' acting it's hard to be sure -- Neo borrows a hovercraft in order to do messiah stuff in Machine City, a menacing mechanized metropolis on the Earth's apocalyptic surface.

Meanwhile, plucky guerrilla pilot Niobi (Jada Pinkett Smith) races back aboard another vessel to the besieged Zion. Neo confronts the machine monarch, which, in a rare injection of humor, is called the Deus Ex Machina -- referring to the device in ancient Greek and Roman drama of a god descending to miraculously save the day. This tongue-in-cheek nod to hokey solutions should clue viewers to the pat ending to follow.

It is hard to root for the home team when, apart from Pinkett Smith, the human leads are just as robotic as their android adversaries. Allegiance to carbon-based life forms aside, what would be worse: a world of Neos or a world of Smiths? At least the pernicious program occasionally cracks a smile.

Early on, it is stated, "There is no action without a consequence" -- unless, of course, one considers the two hours of gratuitous consequence-free mayhem that bookend his remark, including a mammoth battle sequence and the film's operatic, rain-soaked showdown between Neo and Smith. Except for a brief scene in a bar called Club Hell, much of the eroticism that pervaded "Reloaded" has been muted.

Visually, this exercise in bland grandiosity does not make the exponential leaps in special effects that helped the original redefine the sci-fi genre. The pioneering "bullet time" effect, thought so cutting-edge in 1999, is now de rigueur in less lavish films, and even commercials.

As in the two earlier films, "Revolutions" draws themes from a broad range of mythological and theological traditions. Yet much of its metaphysical musings are weighed down by its sturm-und-drang sententiousness and blustering banality. Still, enough breaks through the fray to serve as an opportunity for discussion between Christianity and pop culture, elevating the film above the morass of more mindless action movies.

Due to much stylized violence as well as recurring profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
